stories.title: Russian Peat Held A Carved Face For 12,000 Years
stories.description: Workers pulled a nine-foot wooden idol out of a Ural peat bog in 1890, in ten pieces. In 2021 radiocarbon dating made it the oldest known wooden sculpture on Earth — twice the age of the pyramids. #UnsolvedMysteries #Archaeology #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's best-holding hook (Mirage of Constanz, 187.7% hook hold) states a flat physical impossibility before any context, so this opens on wood surviving 12,000 years and holds the date and place back to the second sentence.

hook_candidates.text: A carved wooden face survived 12,000 years in a bog
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the impossible physical fact — wood that did not rot — with a hard number attached.

hook_candidates.text: This statue is twice as old as the pyramids
hook_candidates.why: Comparison angle; lands instantly but 'this statue' is a vague referent.

hook_candidates.text: Workers found a nine-foot idol in ten separate pieces
hook_candidates.why: Discovery angle, concrete, but the pieces detail is not strange enough on its own.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only candidate whose strangeness is self-evident with zero setup — rotting is what wood does, and the number makes the violation specific.

factual_claims.text: The Shigir Idol was recovered from the Shigir peat bog on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals in 1890, in ten separate pieces.
The idol is carved from larch wood, stands 2.8 m (about nine feet) as reconstructed, and carries multiple carved faces plus geometric ornament; the tree was at least 159 years old when felled.
The Shigir Idol is the oldest known wooden sculpture in the world.
The idol was made by hunter-gatherers, not by a farming or city-building society.
A 2021 study in Quaternary International by the University of Gottingen and the Russian Academy of Sciences dated the idol to roughly 12,000 years ago, far older than Stonehenge.

segments.narration: A carved wooden face survived 12,000 years in a bog. Workers hauled it out of Russian peat in 1890, in ten pieces.
Larch wood, nine feet tall, cut from a tree already 159 years old. Faces stare out of it at several heights, geometric lines running between them.
Nothing else from that era is like it. So who was carving portraits before anyone farmed, built a city, or fired a pot?
The answer is the bog. Peat sealed the larch from oxygen, so it never rotted. Hunter-gatherers made monumental art; we just never had the evidence.
In 2021, new radiocarbon dates put the carving at about 12,000 years old. Older than Stonehenge by seven thousand years.

research.summary: The Shigir Idol, found in the Shigir peat bog near Yekaterinburg on 24 January 1890 and reassembled from ten fragments, is the oldest known wooden sculpture. Carved from larch and standing 2.8 m as reconstructed (Tolmachev's 1914 reconstruction suggested 5.3 m originally), it survived because waterlogged peat kept oxygen off the wood. Successive dating pushed its age from ~9,500 years to the start of the Holocene; a 2021 Quaternary International study by Gottingen and the Russian Academy of Sciences put it at roughly 12,000 years, meaning hunter-gatherers were producing monumental art millennia before farming.

sources.title: This Wooden Sculpture Is Twice as Old as Stonehenge and the Pyramids — Smithsonian Magazine

verification.claim: Found in the Shigir peat bog in 1890, in ten pieces.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives 24 January 1890, Shigir peat bog on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, extracted in ten parts and reconstituted by Professor D. I. Lobanov. Narration says 'workers' rather than naming a finder, because the sources do not name one.

verification.claim: Larch wood, 2.8 m tall, tree at least 159 years old, multiple carved faces.
verification.note: Wikipedia: larch, tree at least 159 years old when felled, 2.8 m (9.2 ft) as reconstructed, multiple faces with additional ones identified by Zhilin in 2014. Narration avoids a face count because sources differ.

verification.claim: It is the oldest known wooden sculpture in the world.
verification.note: Stated by Smithsonian Magazine ('earliest surviving wood sculpture') and by Wikipedia.

verification.claim: Made by hunter-gatherers rather than a farming society.
verification.note: The 2021 dating places it at the end of the last Ice Age / start of the Holocene, before agriculture in the region; coverage of the study describes hunter-gatherer makers. The peat/oxygen preservation mechanism in the same segment is standard bog-preservation chemistry and is not itself tagged as a claim.

verification.claim: A 2021 study dated it to about 12,000 years, older than Stonehenge by millennia.
verification.note: 2021 Quaternary International study (Gottingen + Russian Academy of Sciences); reporting gives c. 12,100 years and notes it predates Stonehenge (c. 5,000 years old) by more than 7,000 years. Narration rounds to 'about 12,000'.

stories.title: Nobody Knows Who Carved This Giant Into Australia
stories.description: In June 1998 a pilot spotted a figure nearly two miles tall scraped into the South Australian desert. Twenty-eight kilometres of lines, no witnesses, and a reward that still has not found the artist. #UnsolvedMysteries #Australia #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's hook-watch examples (Skara Brae 52.2%, Anglo-Zanzibar 51.5%) all drop into a bare date-and-place fragment list right after the hook, so this one keeps the second sentence moving as narrative instead of stacking coordinates.

hook_candidates.text: A man nearly two miles tall appeared in the desert
hook_candidates.why: The scale is the absurdity; 'appeared' does the open-loop work in one word.

hook_candidates.text: Nobody saw anyone carve this 28-kilometre figure
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the absence of witnesses, but 'this figure' needs the viewer to already see it.

hook_candidates.text: Satellites caught a giant appearing in under two weeks
hook_candidates.why: The speed angle; strong but 'giant' reads as a creature before it reads as a drawing.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only one that is instantly absurd without knowing anything — a two-mile man — and it leaves who and how completely open.

factual_claims.text: The Marree Man, a figure about 2.7 km tall, was spotted from the air in June 1998 on a plateau west of Marree in outback South Australia.
The outline is about 28 km long, with lines up to 35 m wide and 20-30 cm deep, and satellite imagery shows it appeared between late May and mid-June 1998.
Anonymous press releases referred to the figure as 'Stuart's Giant', and a plaque bearing an American flag and quoting Hedley Finlayson's 1946 book The Red Centre was found at the site.
Alice Springs artist Bardius Goldberg is the leading suspect, and acquaintances said he claimed to have made it.
Goldberg died in 2002 without publicly confirming it, and a A$5,000 reward offered by Dick Smith in June 2018 did not identify the creators.

segments.narration: A man nearly two miles tall appeared in the desert. A charter pilot found him in June 1998, scratched into a plateau in outback South Australia.
The lines run 28 kilometres, up to 35 metres wide, a foot deep. Satellite images show the whole figure appeared in under two weeks.
Anonymous faxes steered reporters to it, calling the figure Stuart's Giant and quoting an American book. Who builds this, then hides?
Suspicion settled on Bardius Goldberg, an Alice Springs artist who worked at scale and understood GPS. Friends said he admitted it to them.
Goldberg died in 2002 without ever confirming it, and a five thousand dollar reward in 2018 produced nobody. The grader marks are still there.

research.summary: The Marree Man is a geoglyph of a hunting figure holding a woomera or boomerang, cut into a plateau at Finniss Springs about 60 km west of Marree, South Australia. A charter pilot spotted it on 26 June 1998; satellite imagery dates its creation to between 27 May and mid-June 1998. It stands about 2.7 km tall with a 28 km perimeter covering ~2.5 km2, lines up to 35 m wide and 20-30 cm deep. Anonymous press releases called it 'Stuart's Giant' and a plaque with a US flag quoting Finlayson's The Red Centre was found nearby. Alice Springs artist Bardius Goldberg, who died in 2002, is the leading suspect; no creator was ever confirmed, and a A$5,000 reward in 2018 produced nothing. It was restored with GPS-guided graders in August 2016 with the Arabana Aboriginal Corporation's permission.

verification.claim: A figure about 2.7 km tall, spotted from the air in June 1998 west of Marree.
verification.note: Wikipedia: 2.7 km (1.7 mi) tall, 60 km west of Marree, spotted 26 June 1998 by a charter pilot. Narration says 'nearly two miles tall' to match the 1.7 mi figure; some secondary sources give 4.2 km, so the narration avoids a single disputed number and the pilot is left unnamed because sources spell the name differently.

verification.claim: 28 km of lines, up to 35 m wide and 20-30 cm deep, created in under two weeks.
verification.note: Wikipedia: 28 km perimeter, lines up to 35 m wide, 20-30 cm (8-12 in) deep, created between 27 May and 12 June 1998; ExplorersWeb cites NASA imagery for the same window. 'A foot deep' is the top of the cited 8-12 in range.

verification.claim: Anonymous releases called it Stuart's Giant and a plaque quoted an American book.
verification.note: Wikipedia records the 'Stuart's Giant' press releases, the jar of satellite photos and notes, and the plaque with a US flag quoting Hedley H. Finlayson's 1946 The Red Centre.

verification.claim: Bardius Goldberg is the leading suspect and friends said he claimed it.
verification.note: Wikipedia names Goldberg as a suspected creator given his GPS knowledge and access to earthmoving equipment; ExplorersWeb reports multiple acquaintances said he told them he made it but he never confirmed publicly.

verification.claim: Goldberg died in 2002 and a A$5,000 reward in 2018 identified nobody.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Goldberg died in 2002; Dick Smith offered A$5,000 in June 2018 for information identifying the creators, and no one has been identified.

stories.title: France Sent An Army After One Animal In 1765
stories.description: For three years an animal hunted a single corner of south-central France, and the king sent soldiers, bloodhounds and his own hunter to stop it. The man who ended it was a local, and the answer was never a monster. #UnsolvedMysteries #BizarreHistory #France
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hooks (Mirage of Constanz 187.7%, Overtoun Bridge 107.3%) both open on a hard number attached to a repeated event, so this leads with the three-year toll instead of naming the Beast.

hook_candidates.text: One animal killed over sixty people in three years
hook_candidates.why: Number plus an unnamed animal: the scale is instant and the question is what it was.

hook_candidates.text: Louis XV sent royal hunters after a single animal
hook_candidates.why: The absurd mismatch of a king's resources against one creature.

hook_candidates.text: Nobody could agree on what the Beast of Gevaudan was
hook_candidates.why: Names the case first, which only means something to someone who already knows it.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only one that needs no prior knowledge at all and still forces the question the whole video answers: what was doing this?

factual_claims.text: Estimates of the Beast of Gevaudan's death toll run from about 60 to 113 people over roughly three years.
The attacks ran from 30 June 1764 to 19 June 1767 over an area of roughly 90 by 80 km in the Margeride Mountains of the former province of Gevaudan, and a 1987 study counted 210 attacks.

Louis XV sent a force under Captain Duhamel, then the professional wolf hunters Jean-Charles d'Enneval and his son with eight bloodhounds, then his hunter Francois Antoine, who reached Le Malzieu on 22 June 1765.
Antoine killed a large grey wolf, the Loup de Chazes, on 20-21 September 1765 - about 1.7 m long and 60 kg - and received over 9,000 livres, but attacks resumed afterwards.
Jean Chastel shot the animal on 19 June 1767 on Mont Mouchet, and most modern scholars attribute the deaths to one or more wolves, with public hysteria spreading belief in a single monster.

segments.narration: One animal killed over sixty people in three years. It hunted a single corner of France and would not stop.
The attacks began in Gevaudan in summer 1764 and ran for three years, across ninety kilometres of mountains. Reports counted over two hundred attacks.
Louis XV sent soldiers, then professional wolf hunters with eight bloodhounds, then his own hunter Francois Antoine. How does one animal beat all of them?
Antoine shot a huge grey wolf in September 1765, sixty kilos and nearly two metres long, and was paid nine thousand livres. The attacks started again.
A local hunter, Jean Chastel, killed the last one in June 1767. Historians now think it was never one monster, just wolves, and a province that had stopped sleeping.

research.summary: Between 30 June 1764 and 19 June 1767 a series of fatal animal attacks struck the Margeride Mountains in the former French province of Gevaudan, over an area of roughly 90 by 80 km. A 1987 study counted 210 attacks, 113 deaths and 49 injuries; other sources put the deaths at 60 to 100. Louis XV intervened: a force under Captain Duhamel, then the professional wolf hunters d'Enneval and son with eight bloodhounds, then the king's hunter Francois Antoine, who shot a 60 kg grey wolf in September 1765 and was paid over 9,000 livres. Attacks resumed, and local hunter Jean Chastel shot the animal on 19 June 1767. Most modern scholars conclude the deaths were caused by one or more wolves, with public hysteria sustaining belief in a supernatural beast; the silver-bullet detail is a later literary invention.

sources.title: Did a 'werewolf' really terrorize France in the 1700s? - National Geographic

verification.claim: Over sixty people killed across three years.
verification.note: Wikipedia cites a 1987 study counting 113 deaths and notes other sources give 60 to 100. The narration says 'over sixty', which is true on every published estimate rather than picking one disputed figure.

verification.claim: Attacks from summer 1764 for three years across about ninety kilometres, over two hundred attacks recorded.
verification.note: Wikipedia: 30 June 1764 to 19 June 1767, area roughly 90 by 80 km in the Margeride Mountains; the 1987 study counted 210 attacks.

verification.claim: Louis XV sent soldiers, then wolf hunters with eight bloodhounds, then Francois Antoine.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Captain Duhamel led the first force; d'Enneval and his son arrived 17 February 1765 with eight bloodhounds; Antoine replaced them, reaching Le Malzieu on 22 June 1765. Antoine is described as the king's hunter rather than his bodyguard, which is how some popular accounts style him.

verification.claim: Antoine's September 1765 wolf was about 60 kg and 1.7 m long, he was paid over 9,000 livres, and attacks resumed.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the Loup de Chazes, killed 20 or 21 September 1765, about 80 cm high, 1.7 m long, about 60 kg; Antoine returned to Paris on 3 November 1765 and received over 9,000 livres. 'Nearly two metres long' matches 1.7 m.

verification.claim: Jean Chastel killed the animal in June 1767, and scholars now blame wolves rather than one monster.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Chastel shot it on 19 June 1767 on Mont Mouchet; most modern scholars attribute the deaths to one or more wolves or wolf packs, with public hysteria spreading the supernatural account. The narration deliberately omits the silver bullet, which Wikipedia calls a literary invention.

stories.title: America Built A Bomb Full Of Live Bats In 1942
stories.description: A dentist wrote to the White House a month after Pearl Harbor proposing bats as incendiary carriers, and the plan was approved. Two million dollars and one burned-down airfield later, an admiral shut it down. #BizarreHistory #WorldWarTwo #UnsolvedMysteries
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's Hoba meteorite hook (90.9% hold) leads on an impossible outcome and withholds the cause, so this opens on an American airfield burning down and holds back why the bats were armed at all.

hook_candidates.text: Escaped bats burned down an American army airfield in 1943
hook_candidates.why: The outcome is absurd and the cause is missing, so the viewer has to stay for why bats were armed.

hook_candidates.text: A dentist talked the White House into weaponising bats
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the unlikely person behind it rather than on what happened.

hook_candidates.text: Each bomb held a thousand bats wearing tiny incendiaries
hook_candidates.why: Pure device detail; vivid, but it explains itself too early.

hook_choice.reason: It states a result nobody can explain away and keeps the real question - who armed them, and why - open until the end.

factual_claims.text: On 15 May 1943 armed bats were accidentally released at the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico and set fire to the test range.
Dental surgeon Lytle S. Adams of Irwin, Pennsylvania proposed the bat bomb in a letter to the White House in January 1942, about a month after Pearl Harbor.
The carrier was a sheet-metal tube about 1.5 m long holding 26 trays with 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats, each fitted with a small timed napalm incendiary developed by Louis Fieser.
A National Defense Research Committee observer concluded that 'X-Ray is an effective weapon', and the programme was taken over by the Navy as Project X-Ray.
About $2 million had been spent when Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled the programme after learning it would probably not be combat-ready until mid-1945.

segments.narration: Escaped bats burned down an American army airfield in 1943. The bats were armed, and that part was the Army's own idea.
A Pennsylvania dentist had written to the White House a month after Pearl Harbor, proposing bats as incendiary carriers. The plan was approved.
Each casing held 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats in twenty-six stacked trays, every bat carrying a tiny timed napalm charge. Who signs off on this?
The fire happened during a test at Carlsbad. Observers still called the weapon effective, so the Navy took it over as Project X-Ray.
Two million dollars in, Admiral Ernest King killed it: bat bombs would not be combat-ready before mid-1945. The atomic bomb got there first.

research.summary: Project X-Ray was a US attempt to carry incendiaries into Japanese cities on bats. Dental surgeon Lytle S. Adams proposed it to the White House in January 1942; the design used a 1.5 m sheet-metal carrier with 26 trays holding 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats, each glued to a small timed napalm incendiary of Louis Fieser's design. On 15 May 1943 armed bats escaped at the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico, roosted under a fuel tank and burned the test range down. Observers nonetheless judged the weapon effective and the Navy took the programme over, but Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled it after about $2 million had been spent, on the grounds that it would not be combat-ready until mid-1945; the atomic bomb overtook it.

sources.title: Bats carried bombs during this WWII plot - We Are The Mighty

verification.claim: Armed bats escaped and burned down an American army airfield in 1943.
verification.note: Wikipedia: on 15 May 1943 armed bats were accidentally released at Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base, New Mexico, roosted under a fuel tank and set fire to the test range. The narration says 'airfield' rather than naming the base, which segment 4 does.

verification.claim: A Pennsylvania dentist proposed it to the White House a month after Pearl Harbor.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Lytle S. Adams, a dental surgeon of Irwin, Pennsylvania, wrote to the White House in January 1942, a little over a month after Pearl Harbor.

verification.claim: 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats in 26 trays, each with a timed napalm incendiary.
verification.note: Wikipedia: a sheet-metal tube about 1.5 m long with 26 circular trays holding 1,040 bats in total, Mexican free-tailed bats, each carrying a small timed incendiary; Louis Fieser's napalm replaced the original white phosphorus.

verification.claim: Observers called the weapon effective and the Navy took it over as Project X-Ray.
verification.note: The quoted NDRC conclusion 'It was concluded that X-Ray is an effective weapon' is in Wikipedia, which flags some other effectiveness estimates on the page as citation-needed; the transfer to the Navy under the name Project X-Ray is reported by We Are The Mighty. The narration asserts only the verdict and the handover, not any damage estimate.

verification.claim: About $2 million spent; Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled it over the mid-1945 readiness date.
verification.note: Wikipedia: about $2 million had been spent, and Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled the programme after learning it would likely not be combat-ready until mid-1945; the article notes the atomic bomb project overtook it. The narration treats the atomic bomb as the reason it was overtaken, which is how Wikipedia frames it.

stories.title: Viking Swords Carry A Brand Name Nobody Can Explain
stories.description: About 170 Viking-age blades carry the same name inlaid in iron, and seventeen of them spell it wrong. The best of them are made of steel that should not have existed in Europe at the time. #UnsolvedMysteries #Vikings #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's Skyquake hook (125.1% hold) states a plain fact then immediately denies the obvious explanation; this opens on 170 identical signatures and then pulls the brand name apart rather than describing a sword.

hook_candidates.text: About 170 Viking swords carry the same inlaid name
hook_candidates.why: A count plus a signature: it reads as mass production a thousand years too early.

hook_candidates.text: Somebody was faking brand-name swords a thousand years ago
hook_candidates.why: Strongest phrasing, but counterfeiting is a contested reading of the misspellings rather than an established fact.

hook_candidates.text: This blade's steel should not have existed in Europe
hook_candidates.why: Metallurgy angle; 'this blade' needs the viewer to already be looking at one.

hook_choice.reason: It ties with the counterfeit line on score but is flatly true as stated, and the hook has to survive fact-checking like every other claim.

factual_claims.text: About 170 swords (167 catalogued) carry the inlaid inscription +VLFBERH+T.
Ulfberht swords date from the 9th to the 11th centuries and are found mostly in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic, with 44 from Norway.
About 17 known examples carry misspelled forms of the name, such as +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH.
The Frankish form of the name points to a Rhineland origin, and three Ulfberht swords were found in Volga Bulgaria, then part of the Volga trade route.
One Ulfberht example appears to have been made from high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia.

segments.narration: About 170 Viking swords carry the same inlaid name. Ulfberht, spelled out in iron letters down the middle of the blade.
They turn up across Scandinavia and the Baltic, forty-four in Norway alone, made between the ninth and eleventh centuries.
Seventeen of them spell it wrong. Was somebody copying a name they could not read, a thousand years before trademarks?
The name is Frankish, so the workshop was probably in the Rhineland. Three of the swords turned up in Volga Bulgaria, far down the Russian river trade route.
And the best blades are not local metal at all: one is high-carbon steel that may have come from Central Asia. A Frankish brand, foreign steel, seventeen bad spellers.

research.summary: Ulfberht swords are a group of about 170 Viking-age blades, 9th to 11th century, carrying the inlaid Frankish name +VLFBERH+T. Most are found in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic (44 in Norway, 17 in Sweden, 13 in Germany), though the name's form points to manufacture in the Rhineland, with Carolingian capitularia prohibiting sale of such weapons to foreigners. About 17 examples carry misspellings such as +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH, which Stalsberg attributes to illiterate labour in the smithy while also raising the possibility that the signature was copied or falsified. The group spans several steel types and methods; one example appears to be high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia, and three swords were found in Volga Bulgaria on the Volga trade route. Metallurgist Alan Williams' analysis of +VLFBERH+T blades as crucible steel, featured in NOVA's Secrets of the Viking Sword, is the best-known statement of the imported-steel case.

sources.title: NOVA: Secrets of the Viking Sword - KPBS

verification.claim: About 170 swords carry the same inlaid Ulfberht inscription.
verification.note: Wikipedia: 167 found, distribution table totalling 168, lead says about 170, and notes the count is debatable because of fragmentary finds. The narration uses 'about 170' for that reason.

verification.claim: Found across Scandinavia and the Baltic, 44 in Norway, made 9th to 11th centuries.
verification.note: Wikipedia: mostly Fennoscandia and around the Baltic; Norway 44, Sweden 17, Finland 14, Estonia 9, Germany 13; infobox gives 9th to 11th centuries.

verification.claim: About 17 examples spell the name wrong.
verification.note: Wikipedia records about 17 misspelled examples, including +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH. The narration poses copying as a question rather than a finding, because Wikipedia attributes the misspellings to illiterate smithy workers and treats deliberate falsification as an open question.

verification.claim: The Frankish name points to the Rhineland, and three swords were found in Volga Bulgaria on the Volga trade route.
verification.note: Wikipedia: most likely origin the Rhineland based on the Frankish form of the name; three found in Volga Bulgaria, at the time part of the Volga trade route.

verification.claim: One blade is high-carbon steel possibly imported from Central Asia.
verification.note: Wikipedia: one example 'appears to have been made from high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia'. The narration keeps 'may have come from', since the Central Asian or Iranian origin rests on the trade route and metallurgical match rather than direct proof; NOVA's Secrets of the Viking Sword presents Alan Williams' crucible-steel analysis of the same case.

stories.title: An African Spear Solved Europe's Oldest Bird Riddle
stories.description: In 1822 a white stork turned up in northern Germany with a central African spear through its neck, still alive and still nesting. That one bird settled centuries of argument about where birds go in winter. #UnsolvedMysteries #BizarreHistory #Birds
stories.editorial_rationale: Radium Girls' weaker 49.3% hook hold came from an instruction-style opener, so this leads with the physical absurdity itself in the shape of the brief's best hook, Mirage of Constanz at 187.7%.

hook_candidates.text: A stork landed in Germany with a spear through it
hook_candidates.why: A living animal carrying a weapon: strange on its face, and it asks who threw it.

hook_candidates.text: Europeans once believed storks spent the winter underwater
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the old belief, which is funny but makes the video about ideas rather than an object.

hook_candidates.text: One dead bird ended two thousand years of guessing
hook_candidates.why: Teases the significance without giving a single concrete image.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only candidate that puts a hard physical image in front of the viewer, and the spear is the whole evidence the story turns on.

factual_claims.text: A white stork was found in 1822 near Klutz in Mecklenburg, Germany, with a spear lodged through its neck.
The spear was about 75 cm long and came from central Africa, where the bird had been wintering.
Before migration was understood, naturalists held that storks and swallows hibernated underwater or changed into other animals.
Because the spear was identified as central African, the stork must have been wounded there and flown back to Germany.
The stuffed stork is kept in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock, and about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003.

segments.narration: A stork landed in Germany with a spear through it. The bird was alive, nesting, behaving as if nothing had happened.
Mecklenburg, 1822. The shaft ran two and a half feet long, and no hunter in Europe carried a weapon anything like it.
So where had the bird been? Every winter Europe's storks vanished. Naturalists argued they hibernated underwater, or changed into other creatures entirely.
The spear was identified as central African. That meant the stork had been speared there, survived it, and flown thousands of miles home.
One bird proved migration. It is still in Rostock's collection, stuffed, spear included, and roughly two dozen more have turned up since.

research.summary: The Rostocker Pfeilstorch is a white stork found in 1822 near Klutz, then in the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, alive with a 75 cm central African spear lodged in its neck. Until then the winter disappearance of storks and swallows was explained by underwater hibernation or transmutation into other animals, ideas promoted by zoologists of the period. The spear's central African origin showed the bird had wintered there and flown back, which is the physical evidence for long-distance migration. The stuffed specimen is held in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock; about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003, and later cases include a stork from Tanganyika and a honey buzzard from Finland. Audubon's account credits the examination to Heinrich Gustav Florke and places the wound in the Upper Nile region.

sources.title: What This Gruesome Stork Taught Us About Bird Migration - Audubon

verification.claim: A stork was found in Germany in 1822 with a spear through it, still alive.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the first and most famous Pfeilstorch was a white stork found in 1822 near Klutz, Mecklenburg, with a spear lodged in its neck; the whole significance of the find is that the bird flew to Germany after being wounded, so it reached Germany alive.

verification.claim: The spear was about 75 cm long and not of European origin.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives a 75 cm spear from central Africa; 'two and a half feet' is 76 cm. Audubon's account describes tropical wood and a sinew-bound iron tip and gives 80 cm, so the narration avoids the material detail and keeps the length at the figure both sources support.

verification.claim: Naturalists had held that storks hibernated underwater or turned into other animals.
verification.note: Wikipedia: before migration was understood, theories held that swallows and storks turned into other birds or mice or hibernated underwater, and zoologists of the time promoted these ideas. The 'birds flew to the moon' belief appears only in popular retellings and is deliberately left out.

verification.claim: The central African spear meant the bird had been wounded there and flown back.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the spear came from central Africa, where the bird had been wintering, and the specimen showed that birds migrate long distances rather than hibernating or changing form. 'Thousands of miles' is the real distance from central Africa to the Baltic coast and is not a figure either source states numerically.

segments.narration: Oak Island has swallowed 230 years of treasure hunting. Nova Scotia, 1795: a dip in the ground and three teenagers with shovels.
Ten feet down, flagstones. Below that, oak platforms every ten feet, all the way to ninety. Then the shaft flooded and the digging stopped.
Every generation since has tried again. Pumps, drills, a causeway built in 1965 just to haul heavy machinery across. Nothing.
So what is actually down there? Geologists point at the bedrock: limestone and gypsum, the rock that dissolves into caves and then caves in.
In 1878 a farmer's oxen crashed through the ground 120 yards away, into a natural cavern. The money pit was probably a sinkhole all along.

research.summary: Oak Island, Nova Scotia, has been dug for treasure since an often-retold 1795 account of local youth Daniel McInnis noticing a depression. Early companies reported oak platforms down to about ninety feet before flooding stopped work; a causeway was built in 1965 for heavy machinery. Nothing of value has ever been confirmed. The island is a composite of four drumlins with Windsor Group limestone and gypsum bedrock, and skeptics including Joe Nickell and Brian Dunning argue the pit is a natural sinkhole — a reading supported by an 1878 incident in which a ploughing farmer's oxen broke through into a natural cavern about 120 yards from the pit.

segments.narration: A wooden machine beat Napoleon at chess in 1809. Schonbrunn Palace, Vienna: a life-size figure in robes, bolted to a cabinet of gears.
Wolfgang von Kempelen built it in 1770 for Empress Maria Theresa. Before each game he opened the cabinet doors to prove nothing was inside.
It played Benjamin Franklin. It toured London, Leipzig, Havana, Baltimore. Eighty-four years on the road, mostly winning.
So how does a box of cogs read a chessboard? Edgar Allan Poe published his theory in 1836 and got most of it wrong.
A man was folded inside on a sliding seat, reading moves off magnets under each square. In 1827 the operator fainted in Baltimore and two boys watched him climb out.

research.summary: Wolfgang von Kempelen's chess-playing automaton was working by 1769, completed in early 1770, and debuted at Schonbrunn Palace before Empress Maria Theresa. It was exhibited for 84 years, touring France, London, Leipzig and Dresden under Kempelen and later Britain, the United States and Havana under Johann Nepomuk Maelzel. It beat Napoleon Bonaparte at Schonbrunn in 1809 after 19 moves, played Benjamin Franklin in Paris, and lost to Philidor. The machine was not automatic: a human chess player sat concealed in the cabinet on a sliding seat that let him shift as the doors were opened, reading each move from magnets suspended under the 64 numbered squares, with dummy machinery sliding into place to hide him. In 1827 operator William Schlumberger fainted from the heat in Baltimore and two boys saw him leave the cabinet; the Baltimore Gazette reported it on 1 June 1827 and few believed it. The Turk burned on 5 July 1854 in Philadelphia, and Silas Mitchell published the first full explanation in The Chess Monthly in 1857.

segments.narration: One image on 4chan started a fourteen-year treasure hunt. January 4th, 2012. White text on a black square.
Data was hidden inside the picture. Then a phone number. Then websites, ciphers, and paper signs with QR codes taped up in cities worldwide.
The clues quoted Welsh myth, cyberpunk poetry, occult texts. Every one of them was signed with the same PGP key.
Who runs a global cipher hunt and never asks for money? New rounds opened in 2013 and 2014. Then came a runic book nobody can finish.

research.summary: Cicada 3301 posted its first puzzle on 4chan on 4 January 2012; it ran for close to a month. Clues covered cryptography, steganography and internet anonymity and included images with hidden data, a telephone message, websites and paper signs carrying QR codes, alongside references to the Mabinogion, the poem Agrippa and The Book of the Law. Further rounds began on 4 January 2013 and 4 January 2014, the latter posted on Twitter and still unsolved; a further clue appeared in January 2016. Every clue was signed with the same OpenPGP private key, and the last confirmed communication was an OpenPGP-signed message in April 2017 disavowing unsigned puzzles. The runic Liber Primus remains largely undeciphered. Theories about the group range from intelligence-agency recruitment to a cyber-mercenary group, an alternate reality game, or a privacy-focused secret society; the group said it was seeking highly intelligent individuals, and solvers who passed were invited to a private forum and given a project. Its identity and ultimate purpose are unknown.

research.summary: A Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution team first detected a 52-hertz whale call in 1989, and again in 1990 and 1991; in 1992 the US Navy partially declassified its SOSUS hydrophone arrays and made them available for oceanographic research. The call sits at 52 Hz, well above blue whales (10-39 Hz) and fin whales (about 20 Hz), and is shorter and more frequent than theirs. It has been detected every year since, tracking from the Aleutian and Kodiak Islands south to the California coast between August and December; a 2004 study covered twelve years of tracking and noted the call had deepened to around 50 Hz, consistent with maturation. The animal has never been seen. Scientists suggest it is malformed or a blue-fin hybrid; a 2021 documentary included footage of a blue-fin hybrid believed to be the source, and marine biologist John Calambokidis has argued for a part-blue, part-fin animal. Calls picked up by a California sensor in 2010 suggest more than one whale calls at this frequency.

segments.narration: Six hundred nuclear missiles were meant to hide under Greenland. The plan was called Iceworm: four thousand kilometres of tunnels cut into a glacier.
The cover story was science. Camp Century, 1959, a hundred and fifty miles from Thule Air Base, powered by a portable reactor.
Denmark approved a research station on its territory. Denmark was never told about the missiles.

research.summary: Project Iceworm was a classified US Army Cold War plan for mobile nuclear missile launch sites under the Greenland ice sheet, using a tunnel network of about 4,000 km to deploy up to 600 missiles with launch clusters four miles apart. Its cover was Camp Century, launched in 1959 in northwestern Greenland at about 2,000 m elevation and roughly 240 km from Thule Air Base, powered from 1960 to 1963 by the Alco-designed PM-2A portable reactor. Denmark approved Camp Century but never gave consent for missile deployment. The ice sheet deformed the tunnels: by mid-1962 the reactor room ceiling had dropped and had to be raised five feet, and ice cores showed the glacier moving faster than expected. The facility was evacuated in 1965, the camp closed in 1966, and the project was cancelled. Details surfaced from January 1995 during a Danish Foreign Policy Institute inquiry. A 2016 study by Colgan et al. in Geophysical Research Letters found the ice over Camp Century could start to melt by 2100 on current trends, which would risk remobilising buried waste including about 200,000 litres of diesel, PCBs and radioactive waste.

factual_claims.text: In January 2025 Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M. K. Stalin announced a US$1 million prize for deciphering the Indus script.
The Indus script dates to roughly 2800-1900 BCE and survives on about 4,000 inscribed seals, tablets and pottery fragments.
Indus inscriptions are very short, averaging around five signs.
No bilingual or digraphic Indus text has ever been found, and the underlying Harappan language has not been identified.

More than 100 decipherment attempts have been published since the 1920s, with the main competing hypotheses being Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, and a 2004 argument by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel that the signs are not writing at all.

segments.narration: A million dollars is on offer to read five symbols. January 2025. Tamil Nadu's chief minister put up the prize.
The Indus script was written between roughly 2800 and 1900 BCE, across about four thousand seals, tablets and broken pots.
The problem is length. The average inscription runs five signs. Five. There is almost nothing to work with.
And there is no Rosetta Stone. Not one bilingual text has ever surfaced, and nobody knows what language these cities spoke.

More than a hundred decipherments have been published since the 1920s. The serious contenders split three ways: Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, or, per a 2004 paper, not writing at all. Until a longer text appears, five symbols is all anyone has.

research.summary: The Indus script dates mainly to c. 2800-1900 BCE, with possible proto-script traces from c. 3500 BCE. At least 2,906 legible inscribed objects were known by 1977 and about 4,000 by 1992, with a 2025 report putting the excavated total near 5,000 since 1924. Inscriptions average around five signs; sign inventories run from Mahadevan's 419 (1977) to Wells's ~694 (2015). It is undeciphered because the inscriptions are too short, no bilingual or digraphic text has been found, the Harappan language is unidentified, and no Indus rulers or personal names are attested elsewhere. More than 100 decipherments have been published since the 1920s without consensus; the main hypotheses are Dravidian (Knorozov, Parpola, Mahadevan), Indo-Aryan (S. R. Rao), Munda, and a non-linguistic reading argued by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel in 2004 and disputed by Parpola and Rao et al. in 2009. In January 2025 Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M. K. Stalin announced a US$1 million prize for a decipherment.

stories.description: In December 1926 the world's most famous mystery writer vanished, and 15,000 volunteers and the first search aeroplanes went looking. She was found 184 miles away under someone else's name. #agathachristie #1926 #unsolved

factual_claims.text: Agatha Christie's Morris Cowley was found abandoned on 4 December 1926 at Newlands Corner in Surrey, parked above a chalk quarry with its lights on and her clothes inside.
Christie, already a bestselling novelist, vanished from her home in Sunningdale late on 3 December 1926 after a quarrel with her husband Archie, who had asked for a divorce that August.
More than 1,000 police officers, about 15,000 volunteers and several aeroplanes searched for her, the first use of aircraft in a civilian search.
Arthur Conan Doyle gave one of Christie's gloves to a spirit medium, and she was missing for eleven days.

She was found on 14 December 1926 at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel in Harrogate, about 184 miles from home, registered as Mrs Teresa Neele; two doctors diagnosed a genuine loss of memory, and her autobiography never mentions the disappearance.

segments.narration: Her car sat abandoned above a quarry, lights still on. December 4th, 1926, Newlands Corner, Surrey. Clothes across the seats.
The driver was Agatha Christie, already a bestselling novelist. She had walked out of her Sunningdale home the night before, after a row about a divorce.
Over a thousand police searched. Fifteen thousand volunteers. Aeroplanes too, the first time aircraft hunted a missing civilian.
Arthur Conan Doyle handed one of her gloves to a spirit medium. Eleven days passed. The country decided she was dead.

She was in Harrogate, 184 miles north, at a spa hotel, registered as Mrs Teresa Neele, the surname of the woman her husband loved. Two doctors found a genuine loss of memory. Her autobiography never mentions the eleven days.

research.summary: Agatha Christie vanished from her home in Sunningdale late on 3 December 1926, after a quarrel with her husband Archie, who had asked for a divorce in August 1926 because he was in love with Nancy Neele; her mother Clara had died that April and Christie was deeply depressed. Her Morris Cowley was found on 4 December at Newlands Corner in Surrey, above a chalk quarry, with her clothes and an expired driving licence inside. More than 1,000 police officers, about 15,000 volunteers and several aeroplanes searched - the first use of aircraft in a civilian search - and Arthur Conan Doyle gave a spirit medium one of her gloves. On 14 December she was found at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel in Harrogate, about 184 miles from home, registered as Mrs Teresa Neele of Cape Town. Two doctors diagnosed an unquestionably genuine loss of memory; biographer Janet Morgan argued for a fugue state, Jared Cade for a planned disappearance, and Laura Thompson for a nervous breakdown. Her autobiography never mentions the episode.
